Rancid describes food — especially food that contains fat or oil — that has gone stale and spoiled in a very specific, deeply unpleasant way, producing a sharp, sour, and offensive smell and taste.

Think of a stick of butter left out for weeks, a bottle of cooking oil that has been sitting open for too long, or a bag of walnuts forgotten at the back of a cupboard. When the fat or oil inside these foods is exposed to air, heat, or light over time, it breaks down chemically and releases compounds that smell and taste foul — sharp, sour, bitter, almost paint-like. That exact quality is what the word "rancid" captures.

The sensory experience matters here. Rancid food almost always hits your nose first. The smell is not just "bad" — it's offensively sharp and stale, often described as smelling like spoiled milk pushed to the extreme, or like old grease, or even like nail polish remover. The taste, if you're unfortunate enough to experience it, is bitter and deeply unpleasant. Most people feel an immediate, instinctive disgust.

An important point of precision: "Rancid" is not a catch-all word for any food that has gone bad. It is a specific word. It refers primarily to the spoilage of fats and oils. A rotten apple is not rancid — it's rotten or putrid. A rancid piece of cheese or rancid cooking oil has gone bad in this particular fatty, sharp-smelling way. Using the word correctly means saving it for foods with fat or oil content.

The strength of the word also matters. Rancid is not a mild or gentle word. It sits on the stronger end of the unpleasantness scale. It implies something that is thoroughly, offensively bad — not just slightly off or a little stale. When you call something rancid, you're communicating disgust, not mild disappointment.

How it compares to similar words helps sharpen the picture. Stale simply means old and no longer fresh, without the sharp offensive quality — stale bread is flat and dry, but rancid butter is actively revolting. Putrid is even stronger and more graphic, suggesting full decomposition, often used for rotting flesh. Sour refers to an acidic sharpness but isn't tied to fat spoilage. Foul is a broad word for anything deeply unpleasant. Rancid occupies a specific, precise space among all of these: stronger and more offensive than stale, specific to fatty spoilage in its literal sense, and slightly less graphic in its imagery than putrid.

The word also has a figurative life. In everyday language, people stretch "rancid" beyond food to describe anything that feels deeply rotten, corrupt, or morally offensive — something that has deteriorated badly in character. For example: "The rancid attitude of the corrupt official disgusted everyone" or "Years of resentment had left the atmosphere in that office rancid with bitterness." In these cases, the word borrows the feeling of disgust from its food meaning and applies it to people, situations, or environments. This figurative use is fairly common and well understood.
Here are natural example sentences covering both uses:

• The cooking oil had been stored uncovered for months and had gone completely rancid.
  • She opened the fridge and was hit by the rancid smell of old butter.
  • The bag of pine nuts at the back of the pantry had turned rancid.
  • He delivered his criticism with a rancid contempt that silenced the room. (figurative)
  • The rancid odor from the meat told her it had been spoiled for days.

A quick summary to lock it in: Rancid means having a sharp, sour, and deeply offensive smell or taste caused by the spoilage of fat or oil in food. It is a precise, strong word that implies disgust. Beyond food, it can describe anything that feels thoroughly rotten or morally foul. It is stronger than stale, more specific than foul, and slightly less extreme in imagery than putrid.
